The product is good, But, I found that I didn't really need it. - I wanted to push my clothes dryer as close as possible to the back wall. The tight bend in this elbow will allow you to push your dryer closer to the wall without kinking the exhaust hose. This elbow is designed to be attached to the back of your dryer, not to the wall vent. But I guess you could attach it to the wall vent if you wanted to. After I had bought this item (along with a new, semi-rigid, flexible exhaust hose), I found that I could bend the semi-rigid exhaust hose at an angle that was just as tight as this elbow... with no kinks! If your exhaust ducting is made of thin material(as so many are), you may not be able to create a tight bend without creating a kink. Also, if your exhaust ducting happens to be rigid (non-flexible), this elbow will come in handy because of it's tight bend. To reiterate; if your exhaust hose is semi-rigid and can be bent into a tight angle without kinking, you can probably get by without using an elbow such as this one. But, if your flexible exhaust hose is wimpy, this elbow will allow you to push your dryer closer to the wall without having to bend the hose too much.

Convenient for folks who use a lot of ice - There are already two excellent video reviews of this maker, so I am going to fill in the cracks and try not to repeat the product specs or what has already been said. Like the two other reviewers I received my maker as a review sample.

Operationally this is fairly economical since it draws about two hundred Watts (two old style light bulbs.) I do want to set expectations. This will absolutely produce the claimed 26.5 pounds of ice in a twenty-four hour period, but not all at once. Per cycle it will produce a little less than two pounds. A cycle takes up to twenty plus minutes, depending on the ice size that you select. The smaller ice is made a little faster than the largest of the three different 'cube' sizes. Moreover, this will only store a single cycle's worth of cubes, so if you are using it at a party it will require some management of the completed cubes as well as refilling the maker (it takes 2.8 liters of water per cycle.)

The unit is compact and has a few basic operating requirements, like ensuring that the side vents are not blocked. Also, it is not designed for outdoors use, so factor that in if you are purchasing this for a pool party or BBQ.

What it does do, though, is efficiently product ice on a nearly continuous basis as long as you manually transfer the finished ice to insulated coolers as well as keep the reservoir filled between cycles. In that respect the performance is very impressive, and each load of ice is substantial. I am estimating that one of these can easily keep a party of twenty supplied in ice for drinks. Plus, when you factor in the low energy consumption that I cited above this makes an excellent personal ice maker.

Identical to OEM product, just much cheaper - Great tasting water. Identical to the taste from the (much more expensive) Frigidaire OEM filter.

Basically, that's all there is to say. This filter looks pretty much identical to the OEM one (the cap on mine was white instead of blue), and the filtration qualities are identical to it. After running a couple gallons through (necessary for any new filter), the taste coming out is fresh and clean just like the OEM's was when new.

-- UPDATE --

Eight months later, the filter stopped working rather suddenly. We had clean well-filtered water coming through here for just a little over eight months of heavy use by a family of eight who drink a lot of water. Note that eight months is longer than the recommended six-month replacement interval (I missed my phone alarm to change it...), so no complaints on longevity. The sudden change to unfiltered water is actually kind of nice, rather than a slow descent into unfiltered-tasting water; it very clearly reminded me that I'd "slept through" that alarm a few months back! I would recommend buying a multi-pack to have extras on hand in case your usage causes it to stop working before six months is up, and change it at six months regardless (I didn't do that on last purchase because I was suspicious that the much-cheaper filter might not perform as well as the OEM, but now I reordered a three-pack and will keep at least one on hand at all times).

Perfect for my chicken coop! - I’m in Alaska and temps have been -17 F every day for 2 weeks, and it’s only mid-November. With 2 1/2 - 3 months of temperatures like this, my chicken would have serious frostbite and maybe even die, without some heat even in their insulated coop.

We put a radiant oil heater in the coop and use this Inkbird temperature controller to keep the heat at 34 degrees at roost level.
The controller turns the electricity that runs the heater on at 33 degrees, and off at 35. The coop temp has been very consistent and gives me peace of mind.
The floor of the coop is colder so the chickens are still acclimated to below freezing temps, but they get to rest and sleep above freezing which puts less stress in them.

The set up was a little confusing, it helped to read the reviews here to understand what PV, SV, etc meant.
Basically, set the temp for the highest you want it to go which is where you will want the heat to turn off.
Then set the differential to the number of degrees you want the heat to kick on: I set mine at 35 a the max heat I want and where the electricity will kick off. I set the differential at 2, which is 2 degrees less than my max heat of 35. This means the electric will turn on when the coop is at at 33 degrees, and will cut off when the coop temp reaches 35 degrees.

I am very happy with this unit.
